definition: A named, reusable solution to a problem that keeps recurring in software design, described as roles and collaborations rather than finished code. Each pattern comes with its consequences: what it makes easier and what it makes harder.
example: "Wrap this object so it looks like that interface" is the adapter pattern.

definition: Nickname for Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides, authors of the 1994 book Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software. "GoF patterns" means the 23 patterns catalogued in that book.
example: The GoF book splits its 23 patterns into 5 creational, 7 structural and 11 behavioural.

term: Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software
definition: The 1994 book by the Gang of Four that catalogued 23 object-oriented design patterns, with examples in C++ and Smalltalk. It made pattern names part of everyday programming vocabulary.

A 1977 book by the architect Christopher Alexander and colleagues describing 253 patterns for towns and buildings. Its format (a named problem, its forces and a reusable solution) inspired software design patterns.
example: "Light on two sides of every room" is one of its patterns.

definition: An architect whose books on pattern languages for buildings inspired software design patterns.

A design pattern about how objects are created: which class is made, how it is configured and whether a new one is made at all. The GoF creational patterns are abstract factory, builder, factory method, prototype and singleton.

A design pattern about how objects are composed into larger structures, for example by wrapping one object in another. The GoF structural patterns are adapter, bridge, composite, decorator, facade, flyweight and proxy.

A design pattern about how objects share work and communicate: who decides what, and how messages flow. The GoF list 11, including strategy, observer, command, state, template method, iterator and visitor.

term: Program to an interface, not an implementation
definition: A GoF design principle: depend on an object’s promised operations and behaviour instead of one concrete implementation class. A replacement must satisfy the relevant argument, result and error contracts, not merely expose methods with the same names.
example: A report function that only needs out.write(text) works with a file, an in-memory buffer or a test fake.

definition: A class from which another class inherits. A base class may be concrete and usable directly, or abstract with requirements that concrete subclasses must fulfil.
A class that can be instantiated, unlike a class with unresolved abstract-method requirements. A base class can itself be concrete; inheritance alone does not make it abstract.

The operations and behavioural contract an object exposes to callers, including names, accepted arguments, results and expected effects. Java provides interface declarations; Python commonly uses duck typing, abstract base classes or typing.Protocol, with behaviour still needing to meet the caller’s expectations.
example: An object with send(msg) fits a sender interface only if its argument, result and error behaviour meet the caller’s contract.

definition: Using an object according to the operations and behaviour it provides rather than requiring membership of a particular declared class. Matching method names alone is insufficient: argument meanings, results and error behaviour must fit the caller’s contract.
example: A suitable write(text) contract lets a report use a text file, StringIO or a compatible test fake.

definition: In Python, a class using ABCMeta, commonly through abc.ABC, to declare an interface and optionally supply shared implementations. A class with unresolved abstract methods cannot be instantiated; an ABC with no remaining abstract methods can be.
Handing part of a job to another object by calling its method, instead of doing it yourself or inheriting it. Wrappers, strategies and bridges all work by delegation.
example: A Retry object delegates the actual sending to the object it wraps.

definition: An extra layer between the code that asks for something and the code that does it, such as an interface, factory or wrapper. It buys flexibility but makes code harder to follow.

A language has first-class functions when functions are values: you can store them in variables and data structures, pass them as arguments and return them. This is why many patterns shrink to "pass a function" in Python.
example: sorted(words, key=str.lower) passes the function str.lower as an argument.

definition: Java syntax (Java 8 and later) such as String::length that refers to an existing method so it can be passed where a functional interface is expected, much like passing a function in Python.

A Java interface with one function contract that a lambda or method reference can implement. Default methods and methods corresponding to public Object methods do not count as additional abstract requirements; compatible inherited abstract declarations may describe the same contract.
A programming language that does many things at run time that others fix at compile time, such as checking types, adding methods or creating classes. Python, Lisp, Smalltalk and Dylan are examples.
An early, purely object-oriented programming language from Xerox PARC in the 1970s, in which everything is an object. The GoF book used it alongside C++ for its examples.

A compiled language with static types, classes, templates and several programming styles. It supports function pointers and callable objects; modern C++ also has lambdas, so a pattern’s implementation depends on the language features and version available.
A dynamic, object-oriented language designed by Apple in the early 1990s. Peter Norvig used it and Lisp to show how dynamic languages simplify design patterns.

A statically typed, object-oriented language that runs on the Java Virtual Machine. Classic design-pattern examples are often written in Java, which until Java 8 had no lambdas and still has no keyword arguments.
A statically typed language that targets the JVM and other platforms and interoperates with Java on the JVM. Google’s Android development approach is Kotlin-first; Java remains supported.
The programming language of web browsers, also used on servers via Node.js. Its objects inherit directly from other objects (prototypes) rather than from classes.
A dynamically typed, general-purpose programming language with first-class functions and built-in iteration, which make many classic design patterns very short.
Choosing a design pattern before understanding the problem, then looking for places to apply it. It usually produces a shape that doesn't fit.
A code smell: abstractions, hooks or parameters added "in case we need it later" for variation that never arrives. You pay for the indirection now with no payoff.
example: A strategy interface with one implementation that has not changed in five years.

definition: Copying code or structures ritually, without understanding why they were there. With patterns, it means reproducing a whole GoF diagram when only part of it applies.

Introducing a design pattern gradually through refactoring once real variation appears (often the second or third case), rather than designing it in up front. It is the title of Joshua Kerievsky's 2004 book.
example: Turn an if/elif chain into a strategy when the third payment method arrives.

definition: Martin Fowler's 2002 catalogue of patterns for business applications, such as repository, unit of work, data mapper and active record.

An enterprise application pattern that tracks objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates writing their changes and resolving concurrency issues. Implementations may flush changes before the transaction ends; the pattern is broader than one mandatory write at the end.
An enterprise application pattern: a separate layer that moves data between objects and database tables, so the objects know nothing about the database.
example: SQLAlchemy's ORM follows the data mapper style.

definition: An enterprise application pattern in which each object wraps one database row and carries its own save and load methods.
example: Django models follow the active record style: order.save() writes the row.

definition: Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf's 2003 catalogue of patterns for connecting systems with messaging, such as message channel, publish-subscribe and dead letter channel.
An integration pattern: a named queue or topic that one program writes messages into and another reads from, so they never call each other directly.
An integration pattern: a separate channel where a messaging system puts messages it could not deliver or process, so they can be inspected instead of lost.
Patterns for structuring programs that do several things at once, such as producer-consumer, thread pool and reactor.
A concurrency pattern in which one event loop waits for I/O events on many connections and dispatches each to its handler, so one thread can serve many clients.
example: asyncio's event loop and Node.js follow the reactor pattern.

definition: Patterns for the overall shape of a whole system rather than individual classes, such as layered, hexagonal, microservices and event sourcing.
An architectural pattern (also called ports and adapters) that keeps the core business logic independent of databases, user interfaces and other outside systems, which plug in through adapters.

An architectural style that separates concerns into layers, such as presentation, business logic and data access. A strict layered design allows calls only to the next lower layer; more relaxed variants permit a layer to skip intermediate layers.
The Python Package Index: the public repository from which pip installs third-party Python packages.
A GoF behavioural pattern: a request is passed along a chain of handlers until one of them deals with it, so the sender doesn't need to know which one will.
example: Web middleware that may answer a request or pass it on follows this shape.

definition: A GoF behavioural pattern: objects talk to one central mediator object instead of to each other, which reduces how many objects each one depends on.
A GoF behavioural pattern that represents the grammar of a small language as a tree of classes, each of which knows how to evaluate itself.

A GoF creational pattern: a base class calls an overridable method to create an object it needs, and subclasses override that method to choose which class is made. In Python, passing a class or other callable in is often simpler.
example: Django's ListView calls self.get_queryset(); your subclass decides which records it returns.

definition: A GoF creational pattern in which a factory creates a family of related products. Adding a family introduces its factory and matching product implementations; adding a new kind of product affects every factory interface and implementation. Correct implementations and consistent factory use keep the selected family compatible.

A GoF creational pattern: a separate object collects settings step by step and creates the finished object in a final build() call, which can validate everything at once. Python's keyword arguments remove most of the need for it.
example: QueryBuilder("users").where("active").limit(10).build()

definition: A GoF creational pattern: create new objects by copying (cloning) an existing, already configured object instead of building them from scratch. In Python, the copy module provides it.
A variation on singleton that keeps one instance per key in a registry, such as one logger per name.
example: logging.getLogger("app") returns the same logger every time it is asked for "app".

definition: The object-creation operation that selects an instance and sets up its initial state. In Python, __new__ creates or selects the instance and __init__ initialises it when appropriate; in Java, a constructor is a special declaration named after the class, distinct from an ordinary method.

An anti-pattern from languages without keyword arguments: a constructor with a long list of positional parameters, many optional, so calls like User("Ann", null, null, true) are unreadable. Builders were popularised in Java to avoid it.

For a compound object such as a list or dictionary, a copy with a new outer container whose contained objects are shared with the original. Mutating a shared nested list through either container affects that same list; some immutable objects may be returned unchanged by copy.copy.
example: copy.copy(d) gives a new dict whose "tags" list is the same list object.

definition: A copy that recursively copies supported components of an object. Python’s copy.deepcopy uses a memo to preserve repeated-reference relationships and handle cycles, and honours class copy hooks; functions, classes or deliberately shared components may remain shared with the original.
The Python standard-library module providing copy.copy() (shallow) and copy.deepcopy() (deep). It is Python's built-in form of the prototype pattern.
Special methods a Python class can define to control how copy.copy() and copy.deepcopy() copy its instances.
A constructor that builds a new object from an existing one of the same type. Java code usually prefers it to Object.clone().

Python's module for serialising objects to bytes and back. copy.deepcopy falls back on the same protocol (__reduce_ex__) for objects it doesn't otherwise know how to copy, which is why unpicklable objects such as locks can make it fail.
In Python, the class of a class: it controls how classes themselves are created. It can be used to build a singleton, but is the heaviest tool for that job.

The Python special method called to create or select an instance, before __init__ initialises it when appropriate. It can return an existing instance; overriding it is one way to implement a singleton.

A Python module is an importable namespace, often backed by a Python file but also possibly built in or provided by an extension. Ordinary same-name imports reuse the cached module in sys.modules within an interpreter; reloads, cache changes, aliases and separate interpreters limit that sharing guarantee.

The dictionary used as the import system’s cache, keyed by module name. Ordinary imports reuse an existing module entry; deleting or replacing entries can change later imports, and a None entry causes an import failure.
Data that any part of a program can read and change, such as a module variable or singleton. Behaviour then depends on hidden history, and tests leak into each other.
A program-wide lookup table that maps names or types to objects, so code anywhere can fetch them. Service locators and plug-in systems use one; it is global mutable state.
A copy of a database that receives the primary's changes and serves read-only queries, spreading load off the primary.
An object created and managed by the Spring framework's container in Java. By default Spring creates one instance per bean definition per container (singleton scope) and injects it where needed.
A widely used Python database toolkit and ORM. Its select() statements are built up step by step with method calls, builder-style.
example: select(User).where(User.age > 18)

definition: Python's standard interface for database drivers (PEP 249): connect(), cursors, execute() and fetch methods, so code looks similar across databases.

A library that communicates with a particular database and exposes operations through an API such as DB-API or JDBC. Networked databases require the driver to implement that server’s communication rules; embedded databases can run in the same process.
example: psycopg talks to PostgreSQL; sqlite3 talks to SQLite.

definition: A database's particular version of SQL syntax and types. In SQLAlchemy, a dialect object knows how to compile queries for one database, such as PostgreSQL or SQLite.

A standard for remote procedure calls in which method names, arguments and results are represented in XML and carried over HTTP. Python’s xmlrpc.client.ServerProxy makes such requests through local-looking method calls.
A popular HTTP client library for Java and Kotlin, which builds requests with a builder: Request.Builder().url(...).build().
A popular Python web framework with an ORM, templates, forms and an admin site. It uses many patterns: factory methods in class-based views, observer in signals, command in migrations.
Django views written as classes whose methods (get(), get_queryset(), get_form_class() and so on) you override, rather than as plain functions. They use template method and factory method.
A widely used add-on for building REST APIs with Django; its views call get_serializer_class(), a factory method subclasses override.
Django's object representing a database query. It is lazy: the SQL only runs when you iterate over it or otherwise need the results.
example: Order.objects.filter(owner=u) builds a QuerySet without querying yet.

definition: A class method that offers another named way to create an object, such as datetime.fromtimestamp() or dict.fromkeys().
A Python method decorated with @classmethod that receives the class itself rather than an instance, which is how alternative constructors are written.
Existing code that is still in use but is old, poorly understood or awkward to change, often written by people who have moved on.
In JavaScript, every object can have another object as its prototype; property lookups that fail on the object continue on its prototype. Objects inherit from objects rather than from classes.
Python's io module, which builds file objects in layers: a raw binary stream (FileIO), a buffered stream on top (BufferedReader or BufferedWriter), and a text stream (TextIOWrapper) on top of that.
example: open("f.txt") returns a TextIOWrapper around a BufferedReader around a FileIO.

definition: A GoF structural pattern: a wrapper that makes one interface look like another, so code expecting interface A can use a class that offers interface B.
example: An SmsAdapter exposes send(to, msg) and calls the legacy transmit(number, body).

definition: In the adapter pattern, the existing object whose interface doesn't fit and which the adapter wraps.

A GoF structural pattern: a wrapper with the same relevant interface as the object it wraps, adding behaviour before or after forwarding calls. Compatible wrappers can wrap other wrappers, but their order may change results. Python’s @decorator syntax is broader than this object pattern.
example: BufferedReader(FileIO(...)) adds buffering behind the same read() method.

definition: Python's @name syntax, which passes a function or class to another callable and binds the result to the same name. It often wraps the function (like the decorator pattern), but can also just register it and return it unchanged.
example: @functools.lru_cache adds caching to a function.

definition: A GoF structural pattern: a stand-in with the same interface as a real object that controls access to it, for example creating it lazily, checking permissions or forwarding calls over a network.
A proxy that delays creating an expensive real object until a method is first called on it, then reuses it.
example: LazyReport only builds BigReport when total() is first called.

definition: A proxy that makes an object on another machine look like a local one by turning method calls into network requests. It hides failures and latency that callers must still handle.
example: xmlrpc.client.ServerProxy is a remote proxy.

definition: A GoF structural pattern: one simple entry point over a complicated subsystem, covering the common case while leaving the full subsystem available.
example: subprocess.run is a facade over Popen and pipes.

definition: A GoF structural pattern for trees: single items (leaves) and groups (composites) share one interface, so client code treats one item and a whole tree the same way.
example: Folder.size() sums its children; File.size() returns its own size.

definition: A GoF structural pattern separating independently varying abstractions and implementations through composition. Each kind on either side can be implemented once instead of writing a subclass for every pair, provided every pairing fits the shared implementation interface.
example: 4 chart types and 3 output formats: 7 classes rather than 12.

definition: A GoF structural pattern for saving memory: share one object for all the identical (intrinsic) state and pass the varying (extrinsic) state in from outside.
example: A text editor shares one glyph object per character and font, and stores only each character's position.

definition: In the flyweight pattern, the state that is the same for every use of an object and is stored once in the shared object, such as a glyph's character and font.
In the flyweight pattern, the state that differs for each use, such as a character's position on the page. The client keeps it and passes it in.

A visual shape used to draw text, often selected by a shaping engine using a character sequence and a font. Renderers can share compatible glyph data across occurrences while storing each occurrence’s position separately, a flyweight-style design.

Code that holds or calls another piece of code and forwards to it, possibly changing or adding something on the way: usually an object around another object, but also a function or script around another. Adapter, decorator, proxy and facade are all kinds of wrapper.

An anti-pattern: one class that knows and does far too much (validation, pricing, database, email, formatting), so every change risks breaking something unrelated. The AntiPatterns book calls it the Blob.
example: A 4,000-line OrderManager with 90 methods.

definition: Python's text stream class: it wraps a binary stream and turns bytes into str by decoding and handling newlines. open("f.txt") returns one. It is an adapter.
Python's buffered binary stream: it wraps a raw stream such as FileIO and reads in large chunks, keeping the same read() interface. It is a decorator.

Python’s raw binary file stream. A read with a positive size, readinto or write attempts one low-level system call, with retries possible after interruption; reading all data can require several calls. Raw non-blocking I/O may return None when no data is currently available.
A Python in-memory text stream: it behaves like an open text file but stores the text in a string, which makes it a handy test double.

A file-like object whose read and write operations use text strings. A text stream wrapping a binary stream uses a character encoding to convert between strings and bytes; an in-memory StringIO need not encode to bytes.

A file-like object whose operations read or write bytes without text decoding. Files opened in binary mode supply binary streams; sockets and pipes also carry bytes, but their concrete APIs and buffering behaviour can differ.
The rule for turning text characters into bytes and back, such as UTF-8. A text stream needs one to decode the bytes it reads.
Collecting data in memory and reading or writing it in large chunks, so a program makes fewer slow operating-system calls.
example: A buffered reader may fetch 8 KB at once even if you read one line.

definition: A Python HTTP client library. Its convenience functions, such as requests.get, sit above sessions and transport adapters; an explicitly reused Session can share cookies and connection pools across calls.
In requests, the transport adapter that connects requests' session API to urllib3's connection pools. You can mount your own for a URL prefix.
A Python HTTP library providing connection pooling, retries and TLS, which requests uses underneath.

An HTTP client object that can retain settings, cookies and connection pools across requests. Reusing connections may reduce setup work when the server, protocol and pool state allow it; it does not guarantee that every call is faster.
Simple Logging Facade for Java: a logging API that application code calls, with bindings (providers) that route the calls to a real logging library such as Logback or Log4j.
A Java logging library, commonly used behind SLF4J.
An Apache logging library for Java; Log4j 2 can be used behind SLF4J.
A Python decorator that remembers a function's results for recent arguments and returns the stored result for repeated calls. maxsize=None makes the cache unbounded.
A Python helper used inside decorators to copy the wrapped function's name, docstring and other metadata onto the wrapper.
A lightweight Python web framework. Its @app.route decorator registers a view function for a URL and returns it unchanged.
Web Server Gateway Interface: the standard (PEP 3333) for how Python web servers call synchronous web applications. Middleware is a WSGI app that wraps another.
Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface: the async successor to WSGI, used by frameworks that support asyncio and WebSockets.
Java's stream library, the textbook decorator example: new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(f)) adds buffering to a file stream behind the same read() interface.
A performance bug: one query loads a list of N records, then accessing a lazily loaded relation on each runs one extra query per record, N + 1 in total.
example: 100 orders, each touching order.customer, cause 101 queries.

definition: Deferring loading an object or its related data until it is first used. It avoids work that may not be needed, but can hide extra database queries (the N+1 problem).
A Django QuerySet method that fetches related objects in the same query with an SQL join, avoiding N+1 queries for foreign keys.
example: Order.objects.select_related("customer")

definition: A Django QuerySet method that fetches specified related objects in separate queries and associates them with the main results in Python. A simple single relation commonly adds one query; nested relations, generic relations and other lookup shapes can require more.

Not equal to the special null value that represents missing or unknown data. In SQL, a NOT NULL column constraint rejects null entries; it does not by itself validate other properties of a stored value.
Python's module for weak references, which point to an object without keeping it alive. weakref.proxy forwards calls to the object; WeakMethod holds a bound method weakly.
A Django utility class that wraps a function and only calls it when the object is first used. request.user is one, so authentication is looked up lazily.

A Python function that starts a child program, waits for completion and returns a CompletedProcess describing its arguments and return code. Output is included only when requested through capture or pipe options; by default the child inherits the parent’s standard streams.
example: subprocess.run(["echo", "hi"], capture_output=True, text=True)

definition: Python's low-level class for starting a child process with full control over its pipes, for streaming or two-way communication.
An operating-system channel that carries bytes from one process to another, such as a child process's output back to its parent.
example: In a shell, git log | sort sends git's output into sort through a pipe.

definition: A Python machine-learning library organised around estimator interfaces. Estimators provide fit; predictors add predict, transformers add transform, and Pipeline composes compatible steps. Not every estimator is a predictor.
In scikit-learn, any object that learns from data with a fit() method. Models, preprocessing steps and Pipelines are all estimators.
Trying every combination of a set of candidate settings (hyperparameters) for a model and keeping the best. scikit-learn's GridSearchCV wraps an estimator to do it.
Document Object Model: the browser's tree of objects representing a web page. Elements contain elements (composite), and addEventListener registers observers.
Graphical user interface: windows, buttons and other widgets on screen. GUI toolkits such as Qt and Tkinter supply them.
User interface: the part of a program people see and interact with.
A visible element of a graphical user interface, such as a button, text field or frame. Frames are widgets that contain other widgets.
A cross-platform C++ GUI toolkit, also usable from Python (PyQt, PySide). It provides signals and slots and an undo framework.
Python's standard-library GUI toolkit, built on Tcl/Tk.
Scalable Vector Graphics: an XML-based image format that describes shapes rather than pixels, so it stays sharp at any size.
Portable Network Graphics: a lossless bitmap (pixel) image format.
A 7-bit character encoding with 128 codes covering English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters. Uppercase letters (codes 65–90) come before lowercase (97–122).
example: "F" is 70 and "a" is 97, so "Fig" sorts before "apple" by code point.

definition: A standard assigning code points and properties to encoded characters from many writing systems, along with symbols and other text elements. It does not encode every conceivable character; UTF-8 is one encoding of Unicode text as bytes.
Java Database Connectivity: Java's standard API (Connection, Statement and so on) for databases; each vendor ships a driver implementing it, a bridge between API and implementation.
Python's standard logging system: named loggers decide what to record and pass records to handlers that decide where it goes (a file, the console, a network service).

A documented CPython implementation detail: ordinary built-in integer objects for values from -5 to 256 are cached and reused. This is not a language-level identity guarantee or a rule for arbitrary integer subclasses; compare numeric values with ==.

A Python function returning a canonical interned string for a value. Keep and use the returned reference: interning does not rewrite other references, and the API does not guarantee interned strings remain alive forever.
A Python class attribute listing the instance's fields; it can stop each instance carrying its own __dict__, saving memory when there are millions of objects.
The dictionary in which a Python object normally stores its attributes. Each instance having one costs memory.
Whether two references point to the very same object, tested in Python with is (as opposed to ==, which compares values).

A GoF behavioural pattern in which a subject notifies registered observers about changes through a shared callback contract. Strong subscriptions can keep unwanted observers alive when the subject outlives them; explicit unsubscription or a deliberate weak-reference policy manages that lifetime.
example: An order_paid event notifies an email sender and a shipping service.

definition: A GoF behavioural pattern that turns a request into an object holding everything needed to run it, so it can be queued, logged, retried, sent elsewhere or undone. An invoker runs commands; a receiver does the real work.
example: An Insert command with execute() and undo() in a text editor.

definition: A GoF behavioural pattern: save a snapshot of an object's internal state in a separate object so the state can be restored later, for example to undo.
A GoF behavioural pattern: an object delegates its behaviour to a separate object for its current state, and swaps that object when the state changes, replacing long if-status chains.
A GoF behavioural pattern: a base-class method fixes the steps of an algorithm and calls overridable methods for the steps that vary, which subclasses fill in.
example: unittest's run() calls setUp(), your test method and tearDown().

definition: A GoF behavioural pattern: give clients a separate object that walks through a collection one item at a time without exposing how it is stored. Python builds it into the language.
A memory leak in the observer pattern: an observer that is no longer wanted never unsubscribes, so the subject's list keeps it alive and it keeps receiving events.
example: A closed chart window that still redraws on every price update.

definition: A function you pass to other code so that code can call it later, for example when an event happens or a task finishes.
example: button.clicked.connect(handler) registers handler as a callback.

definition: A function registered to run when a particular event happens, such as a click or an order being paid.
In Python, a method accessed on an instance, such as self.redraw. It remembers that instance, so holding the bound method keeps the object alive.
Django's built-in observer mechanism: code connects receiver functions to signals such as post_save, which Django sends when events happen. Receivers are held by weak reference by default.
Qt's observer mechanism: an object emits a signal, and every slot (function) connected to it is called.
example: button.clicked.connect(handler)

definition: A style of programming built around streams of events that you transform with operators such as map, filter and debounce, a generalisation of the observer pattern.
A family of reactive-programming libraries (RxJS for JavaScript, RxPY for Python and others) built on observable streams and operators.
An operator that waits until events stop arriving for a set time and then passes on only the last one, so a burst of keystrokes triggers one search.
A list of executed commands kept in order so the most recent can be undone, and undone ones redone. A new action normally clears the redo history.
A new operation that offsets the effect of an earlier one that can't truly be reversed, such as a refund for a captured payment. Both stay in the record.

A sequence of local transactions that coordinates a business process across services. When required, compensating actions try to offset completed steps; compensation is a new operation that can fail and does not necessarily restore an identical earlier world.

A service that receives and routes messages between producers and consumers using queues, topics or similar channels. Delivery and retention vary: a queue may remove an acknowledged message, whereas a Kafka topic can retain records after they have been consumed.
A Python task-queue library: calling task.delay(args) serialises the call onto a message broker, and worker processes run it later.
Python's standard module for running calls on a pool of threads or processes: executor.submit(fn, *args) packages a call to run later and returns a Future for its result.
A JavaScript state-management library: actions (plain objects describing changes) are passed to reducer functions that compute the new state held in a store.
Files of operation objects describing database schema or data changes, which Django applies in order; many operations can also be reversed.
Qt's undo framework: each QUndoCommand implements undo() and redo(), and a QUndoStack keeps the history.
A Django setting listing password-hashing classes with a common interface. The first hashes new passwords; the others can still verify older hashes.

Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2, defined in RFC 8018: it repeatedly applies a pseudorandom function, commonly HMAC, to a password and salt to make guessing more expensive. Django 5.2’s PBKDF2PasswordHasher uses 1,000,000 iterations; that version-specific setting can change.
A modern password-hashing function (RFC 9106) that is deliberately slow and memory-hungry to resist guessing with GPUs.
A password-hashing function from 1999, based on the Blowfish cipher, with an adjustable cost factor.
Java's functional interface for comparing two objects, passed to sort methods as a strategy.
Python's built-in mapping type: it stores values under keys for fast lookup. A dict of functions is a simple strategy registry.
example: PRICING = {"flat": flat, "sale": ten_off}

definition: Dictionary-style ordering: compare the first characters, and only if they are equal compare the next, and so on. Python compares strings this way by code point.
example: "a" < "bb" < "ccc"

definition: A sort that keeps items with equal keys in their original relative order. Python's sorted() is stable.
A model in which something is always in exactly one of a fixed set of states, and defined events move it from one state to another.
example: A document moves Draft → Review → Published.

definition: A table mapping a state and an event to a next state, making transition rules visible together. In this module’s partial table, a missing pair is treated as an illegal transition; other designs may specify a default or an explicit error transition.
example: (DRAFT, "submit") → REVIEW

definition: A Java library from the Spring project for declaring state machines.
A small Python library that implements the HTTP/1.1 protocol as an explicit state machine for each side of the connection, without doing any network I/O itself.
"Don't call us, we'll call you": framework or base-class code calls your code at the right moments, rather than your code calling it. Template method and callbacks follow it.
A method in a base class or framework that does nothing much (or something default) and exists to be overridden, so you can plug in behaviour at a fixed point.
example: In Report, header() is an optional hook; rows() is required.

definition: A method marked as an abstract requirement that a concrete subclass must resolve. In Python, @abc.abstractmethod participates in ABCMeta’s instantiation checks and may still have an implementation that overriding methods call through super().

Python’s standard-library testing framework. TestCase.run normally calls setUp, the test method and tearDown in order, a template-method structure; if setUp fails, the test and tearDown are skipped, while registered cleanups have separate guarantees.

A Python standard-library module for network servers. After successful setup(), BaseRequestHandler calls handle() and guarantees finish() through finally; if setup() raises, finish() is not called. Subclasses override handle().
Python's thread class: start() creates an operating-system thread that calls run(), which you can override, or pass a target= function instead.
A Python abstract base class: implement __getitem__, __iter__ and __len__ and it supplies get, keys, items, __contains__ and more, built on those three.
A class that provides extra methods for other classes to inherit, without being a complete base class on its own.
An object that returns the items of a collection one at a time. In Python it has __next__(), which raises StopIteration when there are no more; once used up it stays exhausted.
example: iter([1, 2]) gives an iterator; two next() calls return 1 and 2.

definition: An object from which iter() can obtain an iterator, usually through __iter__, or through the older indexed __getitem__ sequence protocol. Lists can supply a fresh iterator for each traversal; iterator objects also count as iterable and normally return themselves.

Python’s iterator protocol requires __next__ to produce the next item or raise StopIteration, and __iter__ to return the iterator itself. iter(x) normally obtains an iterator through x.__iter__, with an indexed-sequence fallback when that method is absent.

A Python generator function is an ordinary def function containing yield; calling it creates a generator iterator without running its body. Advancing that iterator runs or resumes the body until the next yield or termination. An async def containing yield instead creates an asynchronous generator.
example: def count(): yield 1; yield 2

definition: Deferring a computation until its result is needed. A generator function’s body runs when its iterator is advanced, but argument expressions and a generator expression’s outer iterable are evaluated earlier and can fail before iteration begins.
Python's standard module of fast building blocks for iterators, such as chain, islice and groupby.

An object that executes a query and provides access to its result rows, often through fetch operations or iteration. A server-side cursor keeps query or traversal state on the database server and lets the client fetch batches rather than receiving the full result at once.

The C++ Standard Template Library of containers, iterators and algorithms. Iterator-based algorithms can work with different containers when their iterators and elements meet the algorithm’s requirements; not every algorithm accepts every container.
Choosing which code runs based on the runtime types of two objects, not one. The visitor pattern gets it from two single dispatches: node.accept(visitor), then visitor.visit_X(node).
Choosing which method implementation to run at run time from the actual type of the object it is called on. Ordinary method calls in Python and virtual calls in Java and C++ work this way.
In Java and C++, several methods with the same name but different parameter types; the compiler picks one from the arguments' declared (static) types at compile time.
example: visit(Node) and visit(Add) are overloads.

definition: A class attribute listing which fields a positional pattern such as case Add(l, r): should match, for Python's match statement. Dataclasses set it automatically.
A Python decorator that turns a function into one that picks an implementation by the type of its first argument; implementations for new types can be registered from anywhere.

Python's base class for walking a syntax tree from the ast module: define visit_ClassName methods, and generic_visit recurses into children of nodes you don't handle. NodeTransformer can also replace nodes.

A compiler stage that translates a program representation into a target form, such as machine code, assembly, bytecode or another source language. Required checking and optimisation stages depend on the compiler.

A stage that processes a program representation to perform a task such as analysis, optimisation or code generation. It may traverse selected regions, revisit nodes or iterate to a fixed point rather than making exactly one complete walk.
A C, C++ and Objective-C compiler front end in the LLVM project. Its RecursiveASTVisitor is a visitor over its syntax tree.
A JavaScript compiler that rewrites modern JavaScript into older forms; its plugins are visitors over the syntax tree.
A Java compiler feature that runs plug-in processors over annotated code; its API includes ElementVisitor, a visitor over program elements.

A commonly recurring response to a problem that looks reasonable at the time but whose consequences outweigh its benefits, and for which a better alternative is known. The term is commonly attributed to Andrew Koenig’s 1995 writing.
example: God objects, golden hammers and lava flows.

definition: What version control reports when two branches changed the same lines of a file differently, so it can't combine them automatically and a person must decide.
Code with tangled, unstructured control flow and dependencies, which is very hard to follow or change safely.
A system with no discernible architecture, where everything depends on everything. Brian Foote and Joseph Yoder named it in 1997 and called it the de facto standard software architecture.
Martin Fowler's name for replacing a legacy system gradually: put a routing layer in front, move features to new code one at a time, and retire the old system as it empties.

A component in front of one or more back-end systems that decides where each request goes. In a migration it sends each request to whichever of the old or new system now handles it, which makes gradual migration possible.
An anti-pattern: applying one familiar tool or technique to every problem whether or not it fits, from "if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail".
example: Making every data store PostgreSQL and every integration Kafka.

definition: An anti-pattern: dead or half-finished code from past experiments that has hardened in place because nobody is sure it is safe to remove.
example: # TODO: remove after migration (2019)

definition: Code that is never executed, or whose results are never used, but is still kept and maintained.
Making a new variant by copying existing code and tweaking it. Each bug fix must then be found and applied in every copy.

An object identified by its value rather than a separate identity, such as Money(10.00, "GBP"). Value objects are commonly immutable so a value can be shared without unexpected mutation, and they can keep validation and operations for that value together.

Python’s base-10 floating-point type from decimal. Decimal("0.1") represents that input exactly; arithmetic follows a configurable precision and rounding context, so operations such as division can still round. Decimal built from a float preserves that float’s approximation.
example: Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3") is True.

definition: A number represented by a significand and an exponent in a chosen base, rather than an arbitrary exact real value. Python float normally uses binary floating point, which cannot exactly represent most decimal fractions; Decimal uses base ten with its own finite arithmetic precision.
A global registry that code asks for its dependencies, such as locator.get(PaymentGateway). Mark Seemann argued it is an anti-pattern because the dependencies are hidden in method bodies.

A form of dependency injection in which an object receives its collaborators as constructor arguments. The signature makes those dependencies visible, and tests can supply suitable fakes instead of changing a shared global registry.
example: Checkout(gw, db)

definition: The one place, usually at program start-up, where the real objects are created and wired together and passed into each other.
Martin Fowler's term (2003) for domain objects that are only data with getters and setters, while all business rules live in separate service classes, so the rules can be bypassed from anywhere.
Create, read, update and delete: the four basic operations on stored records. CRUD-heavy code mostly moves data in and out with few business rules.
A style of programming built from pure functions and immutable data, combining functions rather than changing state.
Applying design patterns where no real variation or force calls for them, adding layers, factories and interfaces that only forward calls. It is an anti-pattern in its own right.
example: A GreeterFactory whose only product is EnglishGreeter.

definition: A file that is both complex and frequently changed, so bad structure there costs developers time again and again. Adam Tornhill's Your Code as a Crime Scene builds an analysis method on finding them.
Files that keep changing together in the same commits. If they live far apart, it suggests knowledge about one concept is spread out (shotgun surgery).
A count of the independent paths through a piece of code, roughly one plus the number of decision points such as if, while and case. Higher means harder to test and understand.

An application whose main features are released and deployed together as one unit. It can still contain well-defined internal modules and run as multiple replicated processes; one deployable unit does not require one runtime process.
A test that records what existing code currently does, right or wrong, so you can change its structure and notice if its behaviour changes.
Data that a running system reports about itself, such as metrics, logs and traces, used to see how it is actually used.
Operating system: the software, such as Linux, Windows or macOS, that manages a computer's hardware and runs programs.
Short Message Service: text messages sent over mobile phone networks.
Uniform Resource Locator: a web address such as https://example.com/orders/7.
An operating-system endpoint for network communication; a program reads and writes bytes through it.
Python's basic mutual-exclusion lock, which only one thread can hold at a time. Locks can't be pickled or deep-copied.
The Python exception for connection-related failures, such as a refused or reset network connection.
The Python exception raised when a sequence index is out of range, including pop() on an empty list.
A general Python exception for errors that fit no other category, such as a dict changing size during iteration.
The Python exception raised when you use a weakref proxy after the object it pointed to has been garbage-collected.
The Python exception conventionally raised by a base-class method that subclasses are expected to override.
A 2012 attack on TLS and SPDY compression: when secrets such as cookies are compressed together with attacker-controlled text, the compressed size leaks the secret byte by byte.
A 2013 attack like CRIME but against HTTP response-body compression: compressed page size leaks secrets such as CSRF tokens when they appear alongside attacker-controlled input.
Data in its unencrypted form, before encryption or after decryption. It may be text or binary data; the term does not require it to be readable language.

Data produced by encryption. Secure encryption aims to hide useful plaintext patterns, so its encrypted payload usually offers little for a general-purpose compressor to exploit; framing, metadata and the chosen encryption mode can still affect visible structure.

Representing data more compactly. Lossless compression, such as gzip, preserves the original data exactly and exploits patterns or redundancy; lossy compression can discard information, such as fine detail in an image. Random-looking encrypted payloads usually leave little for a lossless compressor to exploit.
A widely used lossless compression format and tool, based on the DEFLATE algorithm.

A lossless compression algorithm and implementation from Meta with tunable compression levels and a broad speed/ratio trade-off. Results relative to gzip depend on the data, versions and chosen settings rather than one universal speed or compression advantage.
A payments company providing card processing for online and in-store payments.
Amazon Simple Storage Service: AWS's object storage service, which stores files (objects) in buckets.
Google Cloud Storage: Google Cloud's object storage service, similar to Amazon S3.
A British software author and consultant known for Refactoring, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture and many widely used terms, including strangler fig and anaemic domain model.
A software engineer associated with Extreme Programming and test-driven development, and a contributor to the code-smells chapter of Refactoring.
A programmer who invented the wiki and coined the technical debt metaphor.
A computer scientist known for C++ work, commonly credited with introducing the term anti-pattern in 1995.
A software author on dependency injection who argued in 2010 that the service locator is an anti-pattern.

An iterable that can provide a fresh independent iterator for another traversal, such as a list. An iterator is itself iterable but normally returns itself from iter(), so it is not re-iterable once consumed.

The object whose changes or events are announced to registered observers. Its subscription and notification implementation determines listener lifetimes, ordering and what happens when a callback raises.

Calling observer callbacks within the code that emits the event, so emission does not return until those calls finish or an exception interrupts them. This can make slow callbacks part of the emitter’s latency and couples failure behaviour to the dispatch policy.

An asyncio object representing an eventual result or exception. It begins pending and may complete with a result or exception, or be cancelled; callbacks and awaiters observe that outcome. This event-loop Future is distinct from concurrent.futures.Future.

Python syntax such as (x * 2 for x in items) that creates a generator iterator. Its outer iterable expression is evaluated immediately; later work runs as the iterator advances, and memory use depends on retained input, output and other state rather than a universal constant-memory guarantee.

A record of application events used to investigate who did what and when, such as an order being approved. Reliability depends on what is recorded, retention, access controls and tamper protection; the phrase alone does not guarantee a complete or permanent record.

The method iter(obj) normally calls to obtain an iterator. A re-iterable collection can return a fresh iterator each time; an iterator’s own __iter__ returns that iterator itself. The older indexed-sequence fallback also allows some objects without __iter__ to be iterable.
An iterator method called by next(iterator) to produce the next item or raise StopIteration when exhausted. A compliant exhausted iterator keeps raising StopIteration on later calls.

Spring’s inversion-of-control container creates, configures and assembles application objects called beans. Singleton scope means one bean instance per bean definition per container; it does not imply one global object across independent containers.
